title: The archer
hookLine: Cicero's Stoic: the archer does everything to aim well, and hitting the mark isn't wholly his (On Ends 3.22)

cards: You spent a week on the job application. You rewrote the cover letter four times. You prepared for the interview.
You were kind to the receptionist. And they gave the job to the manager's nephew. Did you fail?

Most people would say yes, because they score themselves on the result. But yesterday's line raises a hard question. If the result was never fully in your hands, what exactly were you supposed to succeed at?
The Stoics had a picture for the answer, and a Roman writer saved it.

teach.b: It comes from Cicero, in On Ends, a book about what the goal of life is. Cicero wasn't a Stoic himself, but in the third book he lets a Stoic speak: Cato the Younger, well-known for his stubborn honesty.
Cato says, in paraphrase: imagine someone whose job is to aim a spear or an arrow at a target.
Everything he can do, he must do, to aim straight. Choose the bow, set the feet, draw, breathe, release clean. That is his goal, the thing he truly works for.
Hitting the mark, he says, is something to be chosen, but not desired in the same way. Why?

teach.h: THE ARROW BELONGS TO THE WIND.
teach.b: Once the arrow leaves the string, it belongs to the wind. A gust, a bird, a target that moves. The archer can do everything right and miss, or do it badly and hit by luck.
So the Stoics moved the scoreboard: your success is the shot, not the landing. Aim with everything you have.
Then let go, twice: once with your fingers, and once with your heart. That doesn't mean not caring where the arrow lands. Cato still wants to hit.
It means your worth, and your peace, don't ride on the arrow. Back to the application. You aimed well: the rewrites, the preparation, the kindness to the receptionist.
That part was yours, and you did it. The nephew was wind. Tomorrow you can aim again, and you'll aim better for having practiced.

how: People who draw on Stoicism often use Cicero's archer when facing an uncertain outcome: they judge themselves by the quality of their effort and hold the result lightly.

o: aim your best, since the hit isn't wholly yours
a hunter who never misses what he aims at
a soldier who wins by striking first and fast

games.q: what's inside the archer — tap the pairs.
p: the Stoic who speaks in book three

s: he wasn't; in On Ends he lets the Stoic Cato speak.
in the Stoic picture, the archer still wants to hit the target
hitting is worth choosing. his worth and peace just don't ride on the arrow.
the archer succeeds only if the arrow hits
the Stoics moved the scoreboard: success is the shot, not the landing.

games.q: you're the archer. you've chosen the bow, set your feet, drawn and released clean. a gust of wind pushes the arrow wide. how does Cato's Stoic judge the shot?
o: a success: everything that was his, he did well.
bad luck, so it doesn't count.
games.why: the aim was his; the wind was not. by the Stoic scoreboard he did what he set out to do.

practice: Think of one thing you're working on where the result isn't yours to decide: a test, an offer, a hard conversation, someone's recovery.
On the in-breath, picture drawing the bow with all your care and effort; on the out-breath, the release, the arrow gone, the result handed over. Draw and release a few times, then just breathe.

wordCard.voice: The archer. Do everything to aim well; once the arrow flies, hitting the mark is not wholly yours. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the target, the mark an archer looks at. It gives English the word scope.

carryVoice: Your line: aim, then let go. The shot is yours; the wind isn't. One hundred twelve days in.
